prompt.context: Your client is a major sports league called FLC. They organize a national championship and several other smaller competitions. Serving as the only professional men's soccer league in the country, FLC currently has 10 teams. FLC is involved in general league management, which includes setting rules of gameplay, organizing the US National Championship, drafts, matches, referees and deals with sponsors etc. Currently FLC only receives revenues from royalties paid by the teams within the league, and the company is interested in increasing its net income by expanding its operations.
prompt.question: FLC wants to increase its net income by 20% next year. How should FLC expand its operations to meet this target? What investments would you recommend?

clarifying_info.q: What is FLC's current revenue and net income?
clarifying_info.a: This year FLC's revenue was approximately $100M with a 10% net income margin, so $10M NI.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a required return on investment?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, FLC has an ROI (NI / Investment) hurdle rate of 15%.

clarifying_info.q: Can FLC grow its current business organically or raise royalties?
clarifying_info.a: No. For the purpose of this case, assume FLC's current operations and revenue management are fully optimized — no organic growth is possible.

clarifying_info.q: What type of league is FLC — what sport?
What is FLC's only revenue stream?
clarifying_info.a: Royalties paid by the teams in the league.
No, FLC does not own any teams in the league.

clarifying_info.q: Are teams interested in joining the league?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, assume that teams are interested in joining the league for any option chosen.

clarifying_info.q: What costs does FLC incur when a new team enters the league?
clarifying_info.a: FLC is responsible for large upfront commercial, operational, and marketing costs when a new team enters the league. (See Exhibit 3 for specifics.)

exhibits.shows: A table listing FLC's upfront cost in $M to support entry of a new team, broken down by city (San Diego, Atlanta, Detroit, Houston) and sport (Hockey, Baseball, Football, Soccer).

framework: Current business: FLC's existing soccer league — royalties fully optimized, no organic growth possible
Market entry — same business (soccer): expand geographically by adding new soccer teams in cities not currently served
Market entry — different business: launch a new sport league (e.g., football, hockey, baseball) domestically
Other options: women's league, youth league, acquiring a team (conflict of interest if soccer; risky if other sport)
For each option, evaluate: (1) incremental royalty revenue to FLC, (2) upfront costs to FLC, and (3) ROI vs. 15% hurdle rate
Revenue drivers: number of sports fans in the city, average spend per fan, royalty % paid to FLC, FLC's NI margin
Cost drivers: marketing, labor, SG&A — captured in Exhibit 3 upfront costs

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, which sports are viable candidates for expansion based on potential royalty revenue to FLC?
questions.guidance:
Candidate should calculate total royalty revenue FLC would earn from one new team in each sport. Strong candidates eliminate hockey and baseball by inspection (low royalty % and/or low avg revenue); great candidates skip the math entirely. Football and soccer emerge as the top two.

Formula: (# teams benchmark) x (avg rev per team $M) x (royalty %) = total royalty pool currently; for a new team the same avg rev x royalty % is the incremental royalty.

Key insight: Soccer at 15% royalty and football at 10% dominate; baseball (5%) and hockey (2%) are too low to matter.

math.setup: For each sport: Avg Revenue Per Team ($M) x Royalty (%) = royalty per team to FLC
steps: Total existing royalty pool check — Soccer: 10 x $9M = $90M; Football: 10 x $10M = $100M
Hockey and Baseball produce far less royalty per team; eliminate from further analysis
math.answer: Proceed with Soccer and Football only

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, estimate the incremental royalty revenue FLC would earn from adding one new soccer or football team in Atlanta and Houston.
questions.guidance:
Candidate must identify the number of fans NOT currently served (i.e., the fans in cities without an FLC team), apply the projected revenue per fan, multiply by the royalty rate for that sport, then apply FLC's 10% NI margin.

Formula: (New fans in city) x (projected rev per fan) x (royalty %) x (NI margin %) = incremental NI to FLC.

Note: existing FLC soccer league has 10 teams already; the 'new fans' are in cities not currently served. The exhibit shows total fans — candidates should use the full fan count for the new city as addressable market for a new team.

math.setup: (Fans in city [M]) x (projected rev per fan [$]) = new team revenue; x royalty % = royalty to FLC; x 10% NI margin = incremental NI
steps: Atlanta Football: (4M fans) x $40 = $160M... NOTE: casebook uses (4M - 2.5M) x $50 pattern — re-reading: Atlanta football fans = 4M, but casebook shows $125M rev, implying (4M - 2.5M) x $50 = $125M. Use casebook figures.
Atlanta Football: (4M – 2.5M) x $50 = $125M team rev x 10% royalty = $12.5M to FLC x 10% NI margin = $1.25M NI
Atlanta Soccer: (6M – 4M) x $50 = $100M team rev x 15% royalty = $15M to FLC x 10% NI margin = $1.5M NI
Houston Football: (4M – 2M) x $40 = $80M team rev x 10% royalty = $8M to FLC x 10% NI margin = $0.8M NI
Houston Soccer: (5.5M – 4M) x $40 = $60M team rev x 15% royalty = $9M to FLC x 10% NI margin = $0.9M NI
math.answer: Atlanta soccer: $1.5M NI; Atlanta football: $1.25M NI; Houston soccer: $0.9M NI; Houston football: $0.8M NI

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, calculate the ROI for each city-sport combination and determine which meet FLC's 15% hurdle rate.
questions.guidance: ROI = NI / Investment (upfront cost from Exhibit 3). Candidates should compare each option against the 15% hurdle. Football in both cities falls below the hurdle; soccer in both cities meets or exceeds it.

math.setup: ROI = Incremental NI / FLC upfront cost (Exhibit 3)
steps: Atlanta Football: $1.25M NI / $12.5M cost = 10% ROI — below 15% hurdle, reject
Atlanta Soccer: $1.5M NI / $7.5M cost = 20% ROI — above 15% hurdle, accept
Houston Football: $0.8M NI / $8M cost = 10% ROI — below 15% hurdle, reject
Houston Soccer: $0.9M NI / $4.5M cost = 20% ROI — above 15% hurdle, accept
Combined NI from Atlanta Soccer + Houston Soccer: $1.5M + $0.9M = $2.4M
NI growth required: $10M x 20% = $2.0M target — $2.4M exceeds the target
math.answer: FLC should add soccer teams in Atlanta (ROI 20%, NI +$1.5M) and Houston (ROI 20%, NI +$0.9M). Combined incremental NI of $2.4M exceeds the 20% growth target of $2.0M, and both investments clear the 15% ROI hurdle.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the different ways FLC could expand its operations beyond its current soccer league?

categories.name: Geographic expansion — same sport
ideas: Add new soccer teams in underserved US cities (e.g., Atlanta, Houston)

categories.name: New sport leagues
ideas: Note: football has strong revenue potential but requires expertise FLC lacks; hockey/baseball have low royalty yields

categories.name: Vertical integration
ideas: Acquire a team (conflict of interest if soccer; high risk if other sport — FLC lacks know-how)

categories.name: Revenue stream diversification
ideas: Sponsorship and media rights deals at the league level

recommendation: FLC should invest in launching one new soccer team in Atlanta ($7.5M cost, 20% ROI, +$1.5M NI) and one in Houston ($4.5M cost, 20% ROI, +$0.9M NI)
Combined incremental NI of $2.4M represents a 24% increase over current $10M NI, exceeding the 20% target
Both investments clear the 15% ROI hurdle rate; football options were rejected at 10% ROI
Soccer expansion leverages FLC's existing expertise and avoids the operational risk of entering an unfamiliar sport
risks: Customer preferences could shift away from soccer to other sports
Average fan spending may be lower than projected
As FLC grows, upfront and ongoing costs may exceed estimates
Competitive response from other leagues or entertainment options in new cities
next_steps: Begin negotiations with candidate team owners in Atlanta and Houston
Develop initial marketing and communications plan for launch in both cities
Evaluate additional cities for future soccer expansion in subsequent years
Monitor ROI performance against the 15% hurdle and adjust expansion plans accordingly
